newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines stages "most peaceful" local elections.
newsitem.headline: Philippines stages "most peaceful" local elections.

text.p: Housemaids mingled with millionaires as Filipinos on Monday voted in what officials said were the Philippines' most peaceful local elections, setting the stage for next year's battle for the country's presidency.
About 25 million out of 36 million registered voters cast ballots in nationwide polls to pick 335,000 village leaders in the Philippines' 77 provinces, including the capital Manila.
At stake in each of the country's 42,000 villages, called barangay, are the posts of village captain and seven councilmen.
Full results of the poll are expected in two or three days.
The watchdog Commission on Elections has described Monday's elections as a dry-run for the 1998 political battle to choose a successor to President Fidel Ramos.

Commission executive director Resurreccion Borra said the elected village leaders were vital to politicians aspiring to succeed Ramos because they would be the people "who will deliver the votes" from rural areas during the presidential contest.

"This baranggay election is the most peaceful ever because there are no reports of death on election day," commission chairman Bernardo Pardo told a news conference. Twenty-six people died in the last village elections in 1994, he said.

Scattered reports of violence marred voting in some villages, but a fiesta-like atmosphere reigned in other places with mothers taking their children with them to polling centres as though they were out on a picnic, officials said.

In a "battle of millionaires", former trade secretary Jose Concepcion appeared headed for victory over businessman Enrique Lagdameo in the fight for barangay captain of Manila's elite Forbes Park district, according to unofficial partial returns broadcast on Manila radio stations.
About 60 percent of those who voted in the fashionable village were housemaids.
But the run-up to Monday's polls was not entirely bloodless. Police said four people died in the campaign, including two candidates shot dead during the weekend in towns near Manila.

Three grenade-throwing incidents marred Monday's voting in some rural villages. Two grenades thrown at a polling centre and into a house of candidate failed to explode while a third damaged a candidate's house in southern Davao city.
The Philippines has a long tradition of bloody elections, with dozens of people having been killed in previous national and local polls.

Uncertainties have clouded next year's presidential elections because of widespread speculation that Ramos might seek a second term despite a constitutional provision limiting presidents to one six-year term.
The opposition has accused Ramos of instigating a campaign by a citizens group to change the constitution. Ramos has insisted he will step down next year.
At least a dozen politicans have voiced interest in running for president. They include three of Ramos's cabinet ministers and his sister and current senator, Leticia Ramos Shahani.
